channel.title: Coding on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Coding on Best of AI

item.title: Gemini CLI
item.description: Gemini CLI brings Gemini into the terminal as a coding and automation agent. In a project directory, you describe a task in plain language, such as explaining a codebase, fixing a failing test, or building a feature, and the agent reads files, proposes changes, runs shell commands, and iterates. It can search the web, use a context file to learn project conventions, and work with long contexts thanks to Gemini’s large context window.

item.title: Gemini Code Assist
item.description:
Gemini Code Assist brings Google’s models into the developer’s editor. In VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, it suggests code as you type, answers questions in chat, explains and refactors code, generates tests, and helps fix errors. It can take a larger task and make coordinated changes across files in agent mode. Google also offers a command-line version, Gemini CLI, which many developers use directly in the terminal.

For organizations, enterprise editions add code customization, which lets the assistant take into account a company’s private repositories so its suggestions follow internal libraries and styles, as well as security and compliance features, indemnification, and admin controls. It works with Google Cloud tools such as Cloud Shell, Firebase, and BigQuery, and it can review pull requests on GitHub through a companion app.

item.title: GitLab Duo
item.description:
GitLab Duo integrates AI into the places where developers already work in GitLab. In the editor, it suggests code and generates tests, in merge requests it summarizes changes and helps with code review, and a chat assistant answers questions about code, issues, and GitLab itself. For DevSecOps, it can explain security vulnerabilities and propose fixes, and help find the root cause when a CI/CD pipeline fails.

The company has also introduced agent capabilities that can take on tasks across the software lifecycle, such as planning, coding, and review, with human oversight. Because it works within GitLab, it has access to context from repositories, issues, and pipelines, which general assistants lack. Self-managed customers can use it with their own deployment, and organizations control which models and features are available.

item.title: Graphite
item.description:
Graphite is built around a workflow in which large changes are split into small, dependent pull requests. This stacked approach, popular at big tech companies, lets engineers keep working on the next piece without waiting for the previous one to be reviewed and merged. Graphite provides a command line tool and a web interface that make managing stacks simple, which plain GitHub handles awkwardly.

It adds features around review. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing and merging changes in order, an inbox helps reviewers see what needs attention, and insights show how long reviews take. An AI reviewer comments on pull requests to catch bugs and style problems, which matters as more code is written by AI assistants.

item.title: Greptile
item.description:
Greptile is an AI code reviewer with a focus on codebase context. Instead of reading only the diff, it builds an understanding of the whole repository, including how functions and modules relate, so comments can point to impacts in files the pull request did not touch.

It posts review comments and summaries on GitHub and GitLab pull requests. Teams can set rules in plain language, and the system learns from thumbs up and down on its comments to reduce noise. An API allows developers to ask questions about the codebase.

item.title: Beam
item.description: Beam is Reflection’s open sparse mixture-of-experts model, with 501B total and 23B active parameters under Apache 2.0. It is built for coding, reasoning, and agentic work.

item.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro
item.description: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026. It is a 3T-class model with a 1M-token context window, aimed at coding, 3D, financial research, and agentic tasks. A faster Highspeed variant launched the same day.

item.title: Ling-3.1-flash
item.description: Ling-3.1-flash is a hybrid reasoning model from InclusionAI with 560B total and about 25B active parameters and a 1M-token context. It targets agent, search, office, and coding tasks.

item.title: Muse Spark Open
item.description: Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta, with 816B total and 42B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. It targets coding and agentic work.

item.title: Kimi Code
item.description:
Kimi Code is a command line agent in the same family as Claude Code and Codex CLI. You start it in a project folder, describe a task, and it reads files, edits code, runs commands, and checks results, deciding what to do next based on what happens. Permissions let you approve risky actions.

It defaults to Moonshot AI’s Kimi models, which are known for strong coding and long context, and can also connect to other compatible providers. Features include built-in subagents for coding, exploring, and planning, support for the Model Context Protocol to connect tools, lifecycle hooks for automation and safety checks, and an ACP mode so editors like Zed and JetBrains can drive it.

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, 2026, keeping the 1 million token context window of Claude Opus 5 while matching Claude Fable 5.1 on most of Anthropic’s benchmark suite. The main change is cost: Anthropic says Opus 5.5 runs roughly 40% cheaper than Opus 5 on typical workloads, making it a straight upgrade for teams already on the Opus tier rather than a separate product line.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, a week after Claude Opus 5.5. Anthropic says it generates output more than 30% faster than Claude Sonnet 5 while keeping the same API pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached-input reads at $0.20. The context window stays at 1 million tokens.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon
item.description: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, built for long coding sessions, enterprise knowledge work, and cyber defense. It raises the maximum output to 1 million tokens, up from 64,000 on earlier Gemini models, and Google says it leads on 12 of 18 benchmarks tested against GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Access is restricted for now to vetted partners in Google’s Fairwind cyber-defense program, with no public API or general release date yet. Introductory pricing is listed at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4 and $20 once the preview period ends.

item.title: GPT-6 Sol
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol on September 22, 2026, alongside the cheaper GPT-6 Luna, positioning both below the earlier GPT-6 Astra flagship in the GPT-6 lineup. Sol reads up to 1.05 million tokens of context and writes up to 128,000 tokens of output, aimed at coding and agentic tasks rather than Astra’s recurrent-depth reasoning. API pricing runs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a $0.20 rate for cached input.

item.title: Grok 4.7
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026, alongside Grok Build, a terminal-native coding agent built around it. The model keeps the same per-token pricing as Grok 4.6 and offers a 500,000 token context window. Grok 5 is still in training at xAI with no committed release date, making 4.7 an interim update aimed mostly at coding and knowledge-work tasks.

item.title: ByteAsk
item.description:
ByteAsk positions itself around a less glamorous part of software work. Most AI coding tools focus on writing new code, but a large share of an engineer’s time goes into finding why something breaks, why a service is slow, and keeping older systems healthy. A tool focused on that work would read logs, traces, and code to find causes and suggest fixes.

That area is promising because debugging depends on context that general assistants lack, such as how a particular system behaves in production. It also carries risk, since a wrong fix can make things worse, so suggested changes need review and testing before they ship.

item.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash
item.description:
Google pushed out Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, 2026, keeping the same 1,048,576 token context window and 65,536 token output ceiling as 3.7 Flash while posting solid gains on software engineering, agentic, and multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Introductory pricing holds at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens through the end of 2026, after which it doubles to $1.50 and $7.50.

Alongside it, Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a locked-down variant tuned for vulnerability discovery and patching, available only to vetted defenders through the new Fairwind Program rather than the general API.

item.title: Kimi K2.8 Preview
item.description: Moonshot AI rolled out Kimi K2.8 Preview on September 11, 2026, slotting it between the open-weight Kimi K2.7 Code and flagship Kimi K3. It landed inside Kimi Code and Kimi Work the same day with no configuration changes needed, added image and video input on top of text, and bumped every membership tier’s context window from 262,144 to 1 million tokens. Adjustable thinking effort (low, high, or max) now matches the K3 series, with max as the default.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.1
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, 2026, alongside Mythos 5.1, a restricted-access version of the same underlying model available to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences organizations that need capabilities the public release keeps guarded. Fable 5.1 keeps the same $10 per million input and $50 per million output token pricing as Fable 5, but cuts prompt-cache reads from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens, a change Anthropic says lowers effective cost by around 25 percent for typical workloads and as much as 45 percent for heavily agentic ones that lean on cached context. Anthropic reported 52.6 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science as one of the headline benchmark gains over the original Fable 5.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.3
item.description: Meta shipped Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, its biggest coding and agentic jump yet and, according to AI chief Alexandr Wang, a model that closes much of the gap with frontier releases like GPT-5.6. It cuts token usage by 25 percent and tool calls by 20 percent on comparable tasks, and holds the same $1.25 per million input and $4.25 per million output token pricing as its predecessor, plus a contributor tier at a steep discount for developers who let Meta train on their prompts and completions. Access starts through Muse Code and the Meta API, with a “max reasoning” variant still going through safety testing before release, and a rollout to Meta AI, Instagram, and Facebook planned to follow.

item.title: Aloud
item.description:
Aloud addresses the gap between what a developer means and what ends up in a written bug report or feature request. It records voice, screen, and a live transcript while someone talks through an app the way they naturally would, pointing at elements and changing their mind mid-sentence. It then converts the recording into a clean set of instructions.

The output is formatted so coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex can act on it directly. The tool flags anything that could be read two ways and attaches relevant screenshots, which cuts down on back-and-forth. Speech transcription runs locally through Whisper, so recordings stay on the Mac and are not uploaded, which matters for work on client or proprietary code.

item.title: Codex
item.description:
Codex works as a software engineering agent. A developer describes a task, such as fixing a bug or adding a feature, and Codex explores the code, makes a plan, edits files, and runs tests or linters to verify the result. It reports back with a summary of what it changed and why.

It comes in several forms. A command line tool runs on the developer’s machine, a desktop app manages multiple tasks, extensions integrate with editors like VS Code, and a cloud version in ChatGPT runs tasks in isolated sandboxes, often in parallel, and can propose pull requests on GitHub. Configuration files let teams give the agent project instructions.

item.title: GitNexus
item.description:
GitNexus gives coding agents a map of a codebase. It analyzes repositories and builds a graph in which nodes are symbols, files, functions, and services, and edges show how they relate, such as which function calls another. Agents query the graph over the Model Context Protocol to answer questions like what will break if this function changes.

The aim is more reliable context than searching text or embeddings, which can miss relationships. The graph can span multiple repositories, which helps in organizations with many services. It works with different agents and editors, and the vendor claims it lowers cost and errors.

item.title: GLM-5.3-Flash
item.description: Zhipu AI officially revealed GLM-5.3-Flash on August 26, 2026, confirming it as the model previously seeded anonymously on testing platforms under the name “Ox Alpha,” which had drawn over 50 trillion tokens of traffic in five days before anyone knew who built it. It’s a 320-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 18 billion active parameters per token, the first natively multimodal release in the GLM-5 line, combining a hybrid sparse-and-linear attention design with a 1-million-token context window. Zhipu pretrained it on a 30-trillion-token multimodal corpus and says it matches Nvidia GPU-based models on efficiency and token cost while running on domestic Chinese chips.

item.title: Grok 4.6
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, extending Grok 4.5’s coding focus toward longer-running agent sessions and more demanding interactive and visual tasks. The model carries a 500,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and exposes configurable reasoning effort levels from low to xhigh so developers can trade off latency against depth on a given request. xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, with rates roughly doubling once a request crosses that threshold.

item.title: OpenCode
item.description:
OpenCode is a coding agent that works in a developer’s terminal. It reads a repository, plans changes, edits files, and runs commands, with a text interface for conversation. The same engine also runs behind a desktop app, editor extension, and web client.

Provider freedom is the main appeal. Users connect models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others, or open models run locally, and can switch between them. Configuration files add project rules, custom agents, and Model Context Protocol tools, and sessions can be shared.

item.title: Gemini 3.7 Flash
item.description: Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on August 13, 2026, just three weeks after 3.6 Flash, keeping the same 1,048,576 token input window and 65,536 token output ceiling while moving the knowledge cutoff to March 2026. Google credits the gains to developer feedback and algorithmic changes rather than a bigger model, and the benchmark jumps are large: DeepSWE v1.1 climbs from 49.0 to 65.3 percent, FrontierCode 1.1 Main goes from 34.4 to 43.6 percent, and Zapier’s AutomationBench nearly doubles from 17.0 to 30.4 percent. Input pricing is cut in half to $0.75 per million tokens as introductory pricing through the end of 2026.

item.title: GLM-5.3
item.description: Zhipu AI released GLM-5.3 on August 14, 2026, calling it the strongest open-weights coding model available, though the weights themselves are not landing until two weeks after the announcement. It shares its base architecture with GLM-5.2, so the roughly 50 percent jump in coding capability Zhipu reports comes entirely from extended post-training rather than a larger model. The company points to a security angle in particular: GLM-5.3 scored 84.5 percent on CyberGym, a benchmark for finding and validating vulnerabilities from source code, edging out Anthropic’s Claude Mythos at 83.8 percent and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 83.6 percent. Zhipu says internal security teams used the model to surface 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 projects.

item.title: Meta Muse Code
item.description:
Muse Code is Meta’s entry into agentic coding. A developer starts it in a project folder, describes a task, and the agent explores the code, plans changes, edits files, and runs tests, working across a repository rather than on single files. It is powered by a Meta model tuned for coding.

Meta presents it as a lower-cost option next to tools from Anthropic and OpenAI, and it runs from the command line on macOS and Linux. Features such as running sub-agents in parallel aim at larger tasks. The tool was released in beta, so expect changes.

item.title: Gemini 3.6 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3.6 Flash replaced Gemini 3.5 Flash as Google’s default workhorse model on July 21, 2026, part of a three-model July drop that also included Flash-Lite and a restricted Flash Cyber variant, with Gemini 3.5 Pro still not shipped. It keeps the 1,048,576 token context window and 65,536 token output ceiling, moves the knowledge cutoff to March 2026, and uses about 17 percent fewer output tokens than its predecessor while scoring higher on coding, long-context, and computer-use benchmarks, including a jump from 37 to 49 percent on DeepSWE. Output pricing dropped from $9.00 to $7.50 per million tokens, with input still at $1.50 per million and cached input at $0.15 per million. Independent evaluations are more mixed than Google’s own numbers suggest: the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores it even with 3.5 Flash, and community coding tests put it behind GPT-5.6 Luna, Grok 4.5, and Kimi K3 on several tasks.

item.title: Google Antigravity
item.description:
Antigravity is Google’s take on an AI-first coding environment. Instead of a chat panel beside the editor, agents have direct access to the editor, the terminal, and a browser, so they can write code, run it, test the result in a browser, and report back with artifacts such as plans, screenshots, and recordings that show what they did.

Developers can run several agents in parallel and manage them from a control view. Later versions added background tasks that run on a schedule and a standalone command line tool. The environment uses Google’s Gemini models and can work with other models.

item.title: Kiro
item.description:
Kiro is built around spec-driven development. A developer describes a feature, and Kiro produces a requirements document, a technical design, and a task list. The developer reviews and edits these, and the agent then works through the tasks, writing code and tests. The idea is to keep an agent aligned with intent on larger work instead of improvising from chat.

The editor is based on Code OSS, so VS Code extensions and settings carry over. Hooks trigger agent actions on events such as saving a file, steering files give persistent guidance about a project, and support for the Model Context Protocol connects external tools. It uses Claude models through AWS.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.5
item.description: Claude Opus 4.5 is the Opus-tier model Anthropic released on November 24, 2025, and its headline change was price: input tokens dropped to $5 per million and output to $25 per million, a two-thirds cut from Opus 4.1’s $15/$75 rate. It scored 80.9 percent on SWE-bench Verified at launch, ahead of Gemini 3 Pro’s 76.2 percent and GPT-5.1 Codex Max’s 77.9 percent on the same benchmark, and Anthropic added an “effort” parameter that lets developers dial reasoning depth up or down per request. It kept the 200,000 token context window and image input support from earlier Opus releases, and shipped alongside a round of Claude Code updates aimed at longer autonomous coding sessions. Anthropic followed it with Opus 4.6 in February 2026 and Opus 4.7 in April, each holding the same $5/$25 pricing while pushing coding scores further.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.7
item.description: Claude Opus 4.7, released April 16, 2026, is a direct upgrade to Opus 4.6 aimed at the hardest software engineering tasks, the ones where earlier Opus models still stumbled on large, unfamiliar codebases. Pricing held at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, and it kept the 1 million token context window with up to 128,000 tokens of output. It shipped with a new tokenizer that produces up to 35 percent more tokens for the same input text, a tradeoff Anthropic made to improve accuracy on code-heavy prompts. It’s available through claude.ai, the API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

item.title: Claude Opus 5
item.description: Claude Opus 5 is Anthropic’s newest Opus-tier model, released July 24, 2026 at the same $5/$25 per million token pricing as Opus 4.8, half of what the larger Claude Fable 5 model charges for similar intelligence. It ships with a low, medium, and high effort toggle so developers can trade cost against reasoning depth on a per-request basis, plus a faster mode that doubles the price to $10/$50 in exchange for roughly 2.5 times the speed. On SWE-bench Pro it scored 79.2 percent, roughly double the agentic coding score Anthropic reported for the previous Opus generation, and it posted 43.3 percent on Frontier-Bench and 30.2 percent on ARC-AGI-3. It carries the 1 million token context window that has been standard across the Opus line since Opus 4.6, and it’s available on claude.ai, the API, and the major cloud platforms from launch.

item.title: DeepSeek V3.2
item.description: DeepSeek V3.2 is DeepSeek’s update to V3.1, publicly detailed on December 1, 2025 after an experimental preview in September. It introduces DeepSeek Sparse Attention, a fine-grained sparse attention mechanism that cuts training and inference cost while preserving quality on long-context tasks, and the flagship Speciale variant carries roughly 685 billion parameters in a mixture-of-experts layout. The context window sits at 163,840 tokens with up to 64,000 tokens of output, and DeepSeek reports gold-medal-level results on 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad and International Olympiad in Informatics problem sets. API pricing runs around $0.21 per million input tokens and $0.32 per million output tokens, roughly half of what V3.1-Terminus cost, particularly for long-context decoding. Like the rest of the DeepSeek lineup it ships under the MIT license with weights on Hugging Face, and it served as the base DeepSeek built V4-Pro on the following spring.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3.5 Flash launched at Google I/O on May 20, 2026 and immediately replaced Gemini 3 Flash as the default model in the Gemini app, Google Search’s AI Mode, and the Gemini API. It handles a 1,048,576 token input window with up to 65,536 tokens of output across text, image, audio, and video, and Google says it runs about four times faster than other frontier models while beating Gemini 3.1 Pro on several coding and agentic benchmarks, including 76.2 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $9.00 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted 90 percent to $0.15 per million, and dynamic thinking is enabled by default rather than requiring a separate flag.

item.title: GLM-5
item.description: GLM-5 is Zhipu AI’s frontier open-weight model, released February 11, 2026 as roughly a two-times scale-up from GLM-4.5, growing from 355 billion to about 744 billion total parameters while keeping a similar 40 billion active per token in its mixture-of-experts design. It ships with a 203,000 token context window, well short of the 1 million tokens its GLM-5.2 successor would add four months later, and Zhipu trained it entirely on Huawei Ascend chips using the MindSpore framework rather than Nvidia hardware. API pricing starts at $0.57 per million input tokens and $1.92 per million output tokens through Zhipu’s own platform and the WaveSpeed API. It shipped under the MIT license, and coverage at the time framed it as the first frontier-class model from a Chinese lab built on fully domestic hardware.

item.title: MiniMax M2.5
item.description: MiniMax M2.5, released February 12, 2026, extends the coding-focused M2.1 model into general office work: generating and editing Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files and switching between different software environments within an agentic workflow. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 230 billion total parameters and 10 billion active per token, ships with a 204,800 token context window and up to 128,000 tokens of output, and comes in two variants, a standard mode running at roughly 50 tokens per second and a Lightning mode at double that speed. MiniMax prices API access at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.90 per million output tokens, among the cheapest rates of any frontier-class model at release, and it ships with open weights under a modified MIT license for self-hosting.

item.title: Mistral Large 4
item.description: Mistral Large 4 replaces Large 3 as Mistral AI’s proprietary flagship, roughly eight months after that model shipped in December 2025. It’s a 190 billion parameter dense model with a 256,000 token context window, priced at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens through Mistral’s own La Plateforme as well as Azure AI Foundry and AWS Bedrock. Mistral says the gains over Large 3 are concentrated in coding and multi-step reasoning, an area where the company has been trying to close the gap with GPT-5.6 and Claude Sonnet 5 rather than compete on raw scale.

item.title: Figma Make
item.description:
Figma Make lets designers and product teams bring ideas to working form. A user describes an app, or starts from a Figma design, and the AI builds an interactive version using code. They can then edit it by chatting, adjusting on the canvas, or changing the code directly.

Because it connects to Figma, designs, components, and styles can serve as the starting point, which keeps results consistent with a design system. Teams use it to test ideas with realistic prototypes before involving engineering, and to share working demos with stakeholders. Backend features such as data storage let prototypes behave more like real apps.

item.title: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
item.description: Claude 3.5 Sonnet is a text-and-image language model from Anthropic, first released in June 2024 as a mid-tier upgrade to the Claude 3 lineup that matched or beat the larger Claude 3 Opus on most benchmarks while running faster and cheaper. Anthropic updated it again in October 2024 with a version that added computer use, a feature letting the model view a screenshot and control a mouse and keyboard to operate software the way a person would. That update made Claude 3.5 Sonnet one of the first widely available models built for agentic tasks like filling out web forms, navigating operating systems, and running multi-step workflows without a human clicking each button. It kept the 200,000 token context window of its predecessors and priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, positioning it as Anthropic’s workhorse model through much of 2024 and early 2025 before the Claude 3.7 and Claude 4 lines replaced it.

item.title: Claude Fable 5
item.description: Claude Fable 5 is a public, safety-restricted release of Mythos, an internal Anthropic model class that the company unveiled in April 2026 and initially withheld from general availability because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Anthropic made Fable 5 available to enterprise customers and paid subscribers on June 9, 2026, after adding safeguards that redirect queries in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology to Claude Opus 4.8 instead, a mechanism the company says triggers in under 5 percent of sessions. On paper it is the strongest model Anthropic has shipped publicly: 95.0 percent on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3 percent on the harder SWE-bench Pro, and 92.6 percent on GPQA Diamond, with strong results in vision and scientific research tasks as well. It carries a 1 million token context window and is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, double what Anthropic charges for Opus 4.8, reflecting its positioning as a specialty top-tier option rather than a general daily driver.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5
item.description: Claude Sonnet 5 launched on June 30, 2026 as Anthropic’s most agentic Sonnet model yet, built to plan multi-step tasks and use tools like browsers and terminals with less hand-holding than earlier Sonnet versions. It performs close to Claude Opus 4.8 on most benchmarks, including roughly 85.2 percent on SWE-bench Verified and 63.2 percent on SWE-bench Pro, while costing noticeably less, which is why Anthropic and reviewers have framed it as a cheaper way to run coding agents at scale. It carries a 1 million token context window with context compaction to manage long agent sessions, and reads both text and images. Anthropic priced it at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through August 31, 2026, after which it moves to standard pricing of $3/$15, and it is now the default model for free and Pro Claude.ai plans.

item.title: DeepSeek V4-Pro
item.description: DeepSeek V4-Pro is DeepSeek’s flagship model, released on April 24, 2026 alongside a smaller sibling, V4-Flash. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 1.6 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active per token, and it introduces a hybrid attention design combining Compressed Sparse Attention and Heavily Compressed Attention that cuts inference compute and KV-cache size sharply compared to V3.2, letting it handle a 1-million-token context window. The model runs in both a “thinking” mode for step-by-step reasoning and a non-thinking mode for fast responses, and DeepSeek reports it leading open-weight models on math, science, and agentic coding benchmarks, with a SWE-bench Verified score above 80%.

item.title: GLM-5.2
item.description: GLM-5.2 is Zhipu AI’s flagship open-weight model, released on June 13, 2026 under the MIT license. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 744 billion total parameters and about 40 billion active per token, and it ships with a context window of 1 million tokens, far beyond the 128,000-token window of its GLM-4.6 predecessor. Zhipu built it specifically for long-horizon coding agents, training it for months on agentic software engineering scenarios rather than general chat.

item.title: GPT-4.1
item.description:
GPT-4.1 is OpenAI’s April 2025 model, released as an API-only update aimed squarely at developers rather than ChatGPT users. Its headline feature is a 1-million-token context window across all three variants, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 Mini, and GPT-4.1 Nano, an eightfold jump over GPT-4o’s 128,000 tokens. It scores 80.1% on MMLU and 54.6% on SWE-bench Verified, a 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on real-world software engineering tasks pulled from GitHub issues.

OpenAI priced the flagship variant at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens, about 26% cheaper than GPT-4o, while GPT-4.1 Mini undercuts GPT-4o by roughly 83% on many benchmarks. The combination of long context and coding performance made it popular quickly for tools that need to process large codebases or long documents in a single pass, and it effectively replaced GPT-4.5 as OpenAI’s recommended model for API use later in 2025.

item.title: Grok 4.5
item.description: Grok 4.5 is xAI’s model released on July 8, 2026, built with a heavier emphasis on coding, agentic workflows, and knowledge work than earlier Grok releases. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scored 54, placing fourth overall among frontier models while taking the top spot specifically on agentic tool use, and it posted 83.3 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 64.7 percent on SWE-Bench Pro, both benchmarks aimed at real coding and terminal tasks rather than multiple-choice knowledge tests. It carries a 1-million-token context window and handles text and image input, and xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a cheaper $0.50 rate for cached input tokens. It’s reachable through the xAI API console, the Grok app, X, and a wide set of third-party integrations including Cursor, OpenRouter, Vercel, and Microsoft’s Word, Excel, and PowerPoint add-ins. Some coverage framed it as xAI’s answer to Anthropic’s Opus-class models, given the shared focus on long agentic coding sessions.

item.title: MiniMax M3
item.description: MiniMax M3 is an open-weight mixture-of-experts model that MiniMax released in June 2026, with weights on Hugging Face by June 7. It has around 428 billion total parameters with roughly 23 billion active per token, spread across 256 fine-grained experts, and MiniMax bills it as the first open-weight model to pair frontier-level coding ability with a 1 million token context window and native multimodal input across text, images, and video. The lab reports 59% on SWE-Bench Pro and 66% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, benchmarks aimed at long-running coding and agent tasks rather than one-off question answering.

item.title: AICode
item.description:
AICode targets a problem many AI coding tools handle poorly: older systems with hundreds of files and years of accumulated decisions. Where an assistant that autocompletes in a single file struggles, a tool built for legacy code needs to understand how modules depend on each other and what a change will affect.

The pitch includes helping developers navigate unfamiliar code, explain what a function does and why, plan refactors, and write documentation or tests. Teams that inherit a system with little documentation can use that kind of help to get productive faster. Work on large code usually depends on good context retrieval and on careful human review of suggested changes.

item.title: Amazon CodeWhisperer
item.description:
CodeWhisperer was Amazon’s first coding assistant, a counterpart to GitHub Copilot that suggested lines and whole functions as you typed in editors such as VS Code and the JetBrains IDEs. It was trained with a special focus on AWS APIs, so it was particularly good at code that called S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, and other AWS services. It also supported many popular programming languages.

Two features set it apart from early rivals. A reference tracker flagged suggestions that resembled open-source code and showed the license, and a security scan checked your code for vulnerabilities such as exposed credentials and injection flaws. An individual tier was free, and a professional tier added admin controls and higher limits.

item.title: Bito AI
item.description:
Bito started as a chat and code-completion assistant inside VS Code and JetBrains IDEs and as a command-line tool. You could ask it to explain a function, write unit tests, find bugs, or generate documentation, and it used a model of your choice for the answers. Its early appeal was practical convenience: reusable prompts for common tasks and support for working with context from your project.

The product has increasingly centered on code review. The AI Code Review Agent examines pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, leaves comments on issues such as bugs, security problems, and style violations, and summarizes the change for reviewers. It builds a model of the codebase so its feedback accounts for how the changed code fits with the rest, which helps reduce noisy comments. Teams use it to speed up reviews and catch issues earlier.

item.title: Blackbox AI
item.description: Blackbox AI was built for programmers. It offers code completion, a chat interface for coding questions, code search, and the ability to turn a screenshot or image into code. A VS Code extension and a web app made it easy to try, and the free tier helped it reach a large number of developers. Users ask it to explain unfamiliar code, convert code between languages, write functions, and fix errors.

item.title: Claude Code
item.description: Claude Code works as an agent on your actual project instead of a suggestion engine in an editor. You start it in a repository from the terminal and describe the task, such as fixing a failing test, adding an endpoint, or upgrading a dependency. It reads the relevant files, makes a plan, edits code across the project, runs tests and other commands, and iterates on the errors. It asks permission for actions that could be risky, and you can review changes as diffs or through git before committing.

item.title: Codeium
item.description: Codeium started as a free alternative to GitHub Copilot, offering code completion and chat in more than 40 editors, among them VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Vim, and Neovim. Its free individual tier and wide editor support earned it a large user base among developers who did not want to pay for a coding assistant or switch editors. It added features such as natural-language code search, in-editor chat, and support for dozens of programming languages.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit acts as a first reviewer. When a developer opens a pull request, it reads the diff along with surrounding code, writes a summary of the change, and leaves comments on potential bugs, missing tests, security concerns, and style. Developers can reply to its comments and ask it to explain or fix things, so the review becomes a conversation.

Configuration lets teams set rules and instructions in plain language so the review follows their standards. It learns from feedback, and can run linters and security scanners as part of the review. IDE and command line versions bring review earlier, before a pull request is opened.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit gives every pull request a quick first review. When a developer opens a pull request, it summarizes the change, walks through the files, and leaves comments on potential bugs, security problems, performance concerns, and deviations from team conventions. It can also suggest fixes that developers apply with a click and answer questions in the comments, acting like a tireless reviewer available at any hour.

It improves with use. CodeRabbit learns from how reviewers respond to its suggestions and from guidelines the team defines, so comments become more relevant over time. It runs linters and security scanners as part of its review, can use context from the wider codebase, and has an IDE and command-line version for reviewing before code is pushed. It integrates with issue trackers to check that changes match requirements.

item.title: Cursor Composer
item.description: Composer was Cursor’s answer to a basic limit of early AI coding tools, which could suggest a line or edit one file but struggled with changes that touched several. You describe a feature or refactor, and Composer works out which files need to change, writes the edits, and shows them as diffs for you to accept or reject. It can create new files, update imports, and keep related code consistent. The feature later evolved into Cursor’s agent, which also runs commands and fixes its own errors.

item.title: GitHub Copilot Workspace
item.description: Copilot Workspace was GitHub Next’s attempt to rethink how AI fits into the work of fixing an issue. Starting from a GitHub issue or a prompt, it first wrote a specification of the current and desired behavior, then a plan listing the files to change, and finally the code. At each stage, you could edit the text, so you steered the work in plain English before any code appeared. The finished changes could be opened as a pull request or run in a cloud environment.

item.title: Google Jules
item.description:
Jules is designed for the delegating style of AI-assisted coding. You link a GitHub repository, describe a task, and Jules makes a plan, works in a secure cloud virtual machine, and proposes changes while you do something else. It clones the repository, installs dependencies, writes code, runs tests, and presents the plan and results for your review. When you approve, it opens a pull request.

It handles routine, well-defined jobs such as bug fixes, adding tests, upgrading dependencies, updating documentation, and implementing small features. You can run several tasks in parallel, review the plan before it starts, and give feedback while it is working. It is powered by Google’s Gemini models and integrates with GitHub issues and the command line.

item.title: GPT Engineer
item.description:
GPT Engineer was among the first projects to show that a language model could generate a whole working program from a prompt. A user wrote a specification, the tool asked clarifying questions, and then it produced files and code. The open-source command line version attracted a large community of developers.

The founders built a hosted product, gptengineer.app, that let non-programmers describe a web app and see it built. That product was renamed Lovable, which grew into one of the best-known AI app builders. The original open-source repository remains available as a way to experiment with prompt-to-code workflows.

item.title: Mutable AI
item.description:
Mutable AI was a startup building AI tools for programmers. Its VS Code extension offered code completion, refactoring, and chat that could answer questions about a project, and its AutoPilot feature aimed to carry out a described feature across a codebase. The team later became known for turning repositories into readable, wiki-style documentation, which helps developers understand unfamiliar code.

Google acquired the company, and the original Mutable AI site no longer works. The idea of generating a living wiki for a codebase continues in Google’s own products, where documentation tools built on that concept have appeared. Users of the earlier extension needed to move to other assistants, as the standalone service is gone.

item.title: Qodo AI
item.description:
Qodo started as CodiumAI with a focus on tests, and has expanded to quality across the development process. In the IDE, it analyzes a function, understands its behavior, and generates unit tests that cover normal cases, edge cases, and failure modes, which helps developers raise coverage without writing everything by hand. It also offers chat and code suggestions that take the project context into account.

The review side is a major part. Qodo Merge, built on an open-source tool called PR-Agent, comments on pull requests with summaries, potential bugs, security issues, and suggested fixes, and can learn a team’s standards so reviews reflect internal rules. Multi-agent review systems and a context engine aim to understand large codebases, which matters for enterprise teams with many repositories. Integrations cover GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and major IDEs.

item.title: Sourcegraph Cody
item.description: Cody grew out of Sourcegraph’s code search, which indexes entire repositories and lets developers find and understand code across many projects. That context was its main advantage: instead of guessing from the open file, Cody could draw on the broader codebase to answer questions, write code that matched existing patterns, and explain how parts of a system fit together. It worked in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and the web, with chat, autocomplete, and commands to edit and test code.

item.title: Supermaven
item.description: Supermaven was a coding assistant that focused on one thing: fast, accurate autocomplete. Its main claim was an unusually large context window, which let it consider much more of your project than most completion tools when suggesting the next lines. Developers liked how quickly suggestions appeared, and extensions for VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and Neovim made it easy to try. A free tier and a low-priced paid plan helped it spread.

item.title: Zed AI
item.description:
Zed is built for speed. Its editor, written in Rust, starts quickly and stays responsive on large projects, and multiplayer editing lets several people work in the same file with voice and chat.

AI is built in rather than added by extension. Users chat with models in an assistant panel, ask for inline edits, and run an agent that edits code across files, with support for several providers and local models. Edit predictions suggest the next change as you type, and the Agent Client Protocol lets other agents run inside.

item.title: Aide
item.description: Aide was an AI-first code editor from the London startup CodeStory. It was a fork of VS Code, so it looked familiar and could use extensions, but it added a layer of AI that understood the project. You could chat about the codebase, ask for changes across several files, and get completions informed by wider context. It was released as open source under the AGPL license, and the project drew substantial interest from developers looking for an alternative to Cursor.

item.title: Augment Code
item.description:
Augment Code is built for teams with big, long-lived codebases. Its main idea is deep context: the tool indexes the repository and related documentation, so suggestions reflect the project’s own APIs, conventions, and architecture, not generic patterns. That reduces the made-up function calls common with less informed assistants.

It works in the editor with chat, inline completions, and next-edit suggestions that anticipate where you will change code next. Agent features take on larger tasks such as implementing a feature or fixing a bug across files, with the developer reviewing changes. A command line tool and integrations extend it into other workflows, and enterprise options address security and data handling.

item.title: Cosine
item.description:
Cosine aims to act like a teammate on a codebase. It indexes the repository, then takes tasks such as fixing a bug or adding a feature, planning the work, editing multiple files, and running tests. It explains its reasoning along the way so a developer can follow and step in.

The company trains its own models, called Genie, specialized for software engineering using data on how developers work. Tools include a command line interface, an editor extension, and a web app, and it integrates with GitHub for pull requests. It also offers deployments for organizations with security needs.

item.title: Factory AI
item.description:
Factory sells AI agents for engineering teams. Droids take tasks from tickets or chat, explore a codebase, make changes, run tests, and open pull requests for review. Specialized droids handle different jobs, such as code review, incident response, or migrations.

The product works through a command line tool, IDE integrations, and a web interface, and connects to GitHub, Jira, Slack, and other tools so agents fit into existing workflows. Enterprise features address security, permissions, and model choice, with support for several model providers.

item.title: PearAI
item.description:
PearAI is a standalone editor forked from VS Code, with AI features built in. Developers get code completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and inline editing, and can connect their preferred models. Because it is a fork, familiar extensions and settings carry over.

It positions itself as an open alternative to Cursor and Windsurf. The AI layer builds on Continue, an open-source assistant. The project had a licensing controversy early on regarding its use of existing code, which it has since addressed.

item.title: Plandex
item.description:
Plandex works in the terminal and aims at tasks that span many files. It plans a change, builds it up in a sandbox so edits can be reviewed before they touch your project, and supports long context windows to keep track of large repositories. Changes can be rolled back, and different models can be used for different steps.

The team behind it announced that Plandex Cloud would wind down, leaving the self-hosted open-source server and CLI. That means new users need to run it themselves, and development activity has slowed, so check the repository for current maintenance.

item.title: Poolside
item.description:
Poolside focuses on one domain: code. The company trains large models from scratch, using reinforcement learning where the model writes code, runs it, and learns from whether it works. The aim is models that handle real software tasks reliably.

It targets customers with strict security needs, such as defense and large enterprises, and offers deployment in their own environments. Products include a coding assistant and an agent built on its models, and the company has invested heavily in computing infrastructure.

item.title: Refact.ai
item.description:
Refact.ai gives developers an assistant they can control. It offers autocomplete, chat that understands the codebase, and an agent that can carry out tasks like fixing bugs, running tests, and refactoring. It plugs into popular editors.

Privacy is a key benefit: companies can run it on their own servers with open models so code never leaves their environment, or use cloud models. Fine-tuning on a codebase is available in some setups.

item.title: Sweep AI
item.description:
Sweep started as an AI junior developer on GitHub. A user described a task in an issue, and the bot read the code, planned changes, and opened a pull request. The team found it hard to reach the reliability they wanted and noticed that most AI coding attention was focused on VS Code.

They pivoted to a JetBrains plugin for IntelliJ, PyCharm, and other IDEs, offering context-aware chat, multi-file apply, and automated code review. The plugin can run in on-premises settings, which suits companies with security needs.

item.title: Aider
item.description: Aider is a command-line tool for pair programming with a language model. You start it inside a git repository, add the files you want to work on, and describe what you want in plain English. It edits the files directly, shows the diff, and commits each change with a sensible message, so you can review or undo anything the model did with ordinary git commands. That tight git integration is what makes it feel safe to use on a real project.

item.title: Amazon Q Developer
item.description: Amazon Q Developer is the successor to CodeWhisperer, and it is built around AWS knowledge. In VS Code, JetBrains, and other IDEs it offers inline code suggestions and a chat panel that explains code, writes tests, and optimizes functions. In the terminal, it adds autocomplete and a chat that can translate plain language into shell commands. In the AWS console and on chat platforms like Slack, it helps troubleshoot services and explains why a resource is misbehaving.

item.title: biela.dev
item.description:
Biela.dev belongs to the group of prompt-to-app tools. A user describes the product they want, and the platform generates the code for the interface and logic, previews it in the browser, and lets the user request changes in conversation. When satisfied, they can deploy it online.

These tools suit prototypes, internal utilities, and early product tests. They shorten the path from idea to something clickable, which helps founders show investors or customers what they have in mind. Generated code can be exported for developers to continue.

item.title: Bolt.new
item.description: Bolt.new turns a conversation into a working application. You type what you want, such as a booking site, a dashboard, or a small SaaS prototype, and Bolt writes the code, installs the dependencies, and runs the result in a live preview in your browser. You can keep asking for changes, and it edits the project as you go. It is built on StackBlitz’s browser-based development environment, so nothing needs to be installed on your computer.

item.title: Cline
item.description: Cline is an autonomous coding assistant that lives in your editor. You describe a task, and it works through it: reading the relevant files, proposing edits, running commands, and checking the result. It has a Plan mode, where it explores the project and agrees an approach with you, and an Act mode, where it carries the plan out. Each file change and terminal command is shown for your approval, so you stay in control, though you can switch on auto-approval for lower-risk actions.

item.title: Continue
item.description:
Continue is built around choice and control. Instead of locking users to one provider, it lets them plug in the model they prefer, from cloud APIs to models running locally with Ollama, and configure how it behaves with rules, prompts, and context from their codebase and documentation.

The extension offers autocomplete, chat that can reference files and docs, and an edit mode that rewrites selected code. Teams can share configurations and use Continue’s hub for sharing assistants, and the project has expanded to automated checks that run on pull requests. Because the code is open, companies can audit and adapt it.

item.title: Devin
item.description: Devin is designed to work like a junior engineer who can take a ticket and run with it. It has its own cloud environment with a terminal, code editor, and browser, so it can clone a repository, install dependencies, write code, run tests, look up documentation, and keep trying when something fails. When it is done, it opens a pull request with its changes and a summary. You can interact with it while it works, and you can run several Devin sessions in parallel on separate tasks.

item.title: Fabricate
item.description:
Fabricate belongs to the group of prompt-to-app tools. A user describes the application, and the platform generates the interface, server logic, and data storage, then deploys it so it can be used right away. The user keeps refining by asking for changes in chat.

It is meant for prototypes, internal tools, and simple products. Getting from idea to something usable in minutes helps founders test concepts. Generated applications need testing, and authentication, payments, and security deserve a careful look before launch with real users.

item.title: JetBrains AI Assistant
item.description: JetBrains AI Assistant works inside the IDEs that many professional developers already use. In IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, Rider, and the rest of the family, it provides inline completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and actions to explain code, generate tests, write commit messages, and suggest fixes for errors. Because it is built into the IDE, it can use the IDE’s deep knowledge of code structure, such as types, references, and run configurations.

item.title: Lovable
item.description: Lovable lets people describe an app and get something that runs. You type what you want, such as a task tracker, a booking tool, or a customer portal, and it generates a React front end, sets up pages and components, and shows a live preview. You then keep chatting to change the layout, add features, or fix problems. It is popular with founders, designers, and product managers who want a prototype without a development team.

item.title: Rocket
item.description:
Rocket belongs to the prompt-to-app builders. A user describes the product, and the platform generates the interface, back end logic, and database, previews it, and deploys it. Further changes are made through conversation, with the option to edit code.

It targets founders and operators who want to test an idea or build an internal tool without engineers. As with similar tools, generated apps need testing, and security and data handling deserve review before real users arrive.

item.title: v0 by Vercel
item.description: v0 started as a tool for generating user interface components from text. You described a pricing table or dashboard, and it produced React code styled with Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui components that you could copy into a project. It has since grown into a full app builder: you can ask for pages, forms, and logic, upload a wireframe or screenshot to recreate, and watch a live preview update as you refine the result in conversation.

item.title: Windsurf
item.description: Windsurf was built by the Codeium team as an editor designed around AI from the start, in contrast to adding assistants to an existing IDE. Its Cascade agent understands the project, edits multiple files, runs terminal commands, and reasons about changes while you watch. A fast Tab completion feature predicts what you will write next, and previews let you see a running web app inside the editor and ask for changes visually. It started from VS Code, so extensions and settings carry over.
